title: Acis et Galatea. Polyphemus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Galatea tells how Acis, the sixteen-year-old son of Faunus and a river-nymph, had bound her to himself alone, and how the Cyclops Polyphemus courted her without ever leaving off. Hidden on a rock in Acis's lap, she heard the whole of the song he sang from a headland with his hundred-reed pipe: praise of her, abuse of her, an inventory of his caves, fruit, flocks and two bear cubs, and a threat to drag Acis's entrails out alive and scatter his dismembered limbs through her water. Then he caught sight of the two of them and threw a piece torn out of the mountain, and Galatea did the one thing the fates allowed, turning the blood that ran from under the mass into the river that kept his name.

sentences.t:
“Acis erat Fauno nymphaque Symaethide cretus,
magna quidem patrisque sui matrisque voluptas,
nostra tamen maior: nam me sibi iunxerat uni.
sentences.l: Acis there was, sprung from Faunus and a Symaethian nymph, a great delight indeed of his father and of his mother, but a greater one of mine: for he had joined me to himself alone.
sentences.i: There was Acis, born of Faunus and the nymph of Symaethus — a great delight to his father and his mother, yes, but a greater one to me: he had bound me to himself and to nobody else.
sentences.n: cretus, “sprung”, takes the plain ablative of origin, Fauno … nympha Symaethide, where English wants “from”. In me sibi iunxerat uni the accusative me is the object and sibi uni the dative: uni can only agree with sibi, so he joined me to himself alone, and not himself to me. Symaethide is the Greek-declined feminine ablative of Symaethis, the nymph of the Sicilian river Symaethus; the name comes back at 879, where Acis is called Symaethius heros. voluptas is not repeated with nostra … maior — the reader carries the noun over from 751 into 752. The edition opens the quotation mark here at 750 and does not close it until the last word of 897: everything in these lines is Galatea speaking.

sentences.t:
Pulcher et octonis iterum natalibus actis
signarat teneras dubia lanugine malas.
sentences.l: Beautiful, and with eight birthdays passed a second time, he had marked his tender cheeks with a doubtful down.
sentences.i: He was beautiful, and with twice eight birthdays gone by he had begun to mark his soft cheeks with a hesitant first down.
sentences.n: natalibus actis is the first ablative absolute in this part: a self-contained “with X done” phrase where English wants a clause. octonis is the distributive, “eight at a time”, and with iterum it counts the birthdays twice over: he is sixteen. signarat is syncopated for signaverat; the verb is active and Acis is its subject, so the literal keeps him doing the marking. dubia, “doubtful, hesitant”, is the down that is barely there yet.

sentences.t: Hunc ego, me Cyclops nulla cum fine petebat.
sentences.l: Him I, me the Cyclops with no end pursued.
sentences.i: Him I wanted; me the Cyclops wanted, and never left off.
sentences.n: One verb serves both halves. petebat is singular and belongs to Cyclops; with Hunc ego the reader supplies petebam, “I pursued him”. The two pairs run parallel rather than crosswise — accusative then nominative, twice over — and the arrangement leaves ego and me touching at the centre of the line, so the two pursuits stand side by side. petere here is “make for, go after, court”. nulla cum fine puts the preposition between the adjective and its noun.

sentences.t:
En si quaesieris, odium Cyclopis, amorne
Acidis in nobis fuerit praesentior, edam:
par utrumque fuit.
sentences.l: Look, if you should ask whether hatred of the Cyclops or love of Acis was the more present in me, I will declare it: the two were equal.
sentences.i: Look — if you were to ask which was stronger in me, my hatred of the Cyclops or my love for Acis, I will tell you: the two were equal.
sentences.n: quaesieris is a syncopated future perfect, quaesiveris, “if you will have asked” — Latin puts the asking finished before the telling begins, where English uses a plain present. What follows is a double indirect question with the subjunctive fuerit, the alternative marked by -ne fastened to amor: “whether … or …”. praesentior is “more present, more immediately felt”, and it is that comparative that carries the sense of “stronger”. edam is the future of edo, edere, “put forth, declare”, not the verb for eating. Magnus prints En, “Look”; some editions print nec, “nor will I declare”, which makes what follows a refusal to choose between the two rather than the declaration edam promises.

sentences.t:
Pro quanta potentia regni
est, Venus alma, tui!
sentences.l: Ah, how great the power of your kingdom is, nurturing Venus!
sentences.i: Ah, kind Venus, how great the power of your realm is!
sentences.n: pro here is the interjection, “ah!, oh!”, not the preposition; it heads the exclamation that quanta completes. The possessive tui, genitive in agreement with regni, is torn a long way from that noun: regni closes 758, and tui does not arrive until after the verb and the vocative in 759. alma, “nourishing, fostering”, is a standing epithet of Venus.

sentences.t:
Nempe ille inmitis et ipsis
horrendus silvis et visus ab hospite nullo
impune et magni cum dis contemptor Olympi,
sentences.l: Surely he — pitiless, and to be shuddered at even by the woods themselves, and seen by no stranger without paying for it, and, together with the gods, a despiser of great Olympus —
sentences.i: He, of all people — pitiless, a thing the very woods shuddered at, whom no stranger ever saw and got off unpunished, who despised great Olympus and the gods along with it —
sentences.n: A pile of nominatives in apposition to ille, with the verb held back into the next unit. horrendus is a gerundive used as an adjective, “to be shuddered at”, with silvis as its dative of agent. impune, “without paying for it”, goes with visus: nobody who saw him escaped the cost. contemptor governs the objective genitive Olympi, and magni … Olympi is split around cum dis contemptor, the adjective early in 761 and its noun the last word of the line.

sentences.t:
quid sit amor, sensit validaque cupidine captus
uritur, oblitus pecorum antrorumque suorum.
sentences.l: he felt what love is, and, seized by a strong desire, he burns, forgetful of his flocks and his own caves.
sentences.i: he found out what love is, and, gripped by a violent longing, he burns — his flocks and his caves forgotten.
sentences.n: quid sit amor is an indirect question with the subjunctive, the object of sensit. The tense then shifts inside the sentence: the perfect sensit gives way to the present uritur, and the burning becomes something still going on. oblitus is the perfect participle of the deponent obliviscor, active in force, with the genitives pecorum and antrorum. Magnus prints sensit; some editions print sentit, present, which levels out that shift.

sentences.t:
Iamque tibi formae, iamque est tibi cura placendi,
iam rigidos pectis rastris, Polypheme, capillos,
iam libet hirsutam tibi falce recidere barbam
et spectare feros in aqua et componere vultus.
sentences.l: And now there is to you a care for your looks, and now there is to you a care for pleasing; now you comb your stiff hair with rakes, Polyphemus, now it pleases you to cut back your shaggy beard with a sickle, and to look at your fierce face in the water and to compose it.
sentences.i: And now you care how you look, now you care about pleasing; now you rake your stiff hair into order, Polyphemus, now you take a sickle to your shaggy beard, and study your savage face in the water and arrange it.
sentences.n: Galatea breaks off from telling the story and speaks to Polyphemus himself: the second-person verbs and the vocative Polypheme run to the end of 767, and the third person returns at 768. iam is counted off four times, twice in 764 and once each in 765 and 766. tibi is a dative of possession in both halves, “there is to you”, which is why the literal keeps that shape twice over; formae and placendi are both genitives after cura, a noun and a gerund doing the same work. rastris, “with rakes”, is an ablative of means, a farm tool turned on a head. libet is impersonal, with tibi and the three infinitives recidere, spectare, componere.

sentences.t:
Caedis amor feritasque sitisque inmensa cruoris
cessant, et tutae veniunt abeuntque carinae.
sentences.l: Love of slaughter and wildness and the measureless thirst for gore cease, and the keels come and go safe.
sentences.i: His love of slaughter, his savagery, his boundless thirst for blood all stop; ships come and go unharmed.
sentences.n: Three subjects strung on -que … -que take the one plural verb cessant. caedis and cruoris are objective genitives: the love is of slaughter, the thirst is for gore. carinae, “keels”, is the part standing for the ship. tutae is a predicative adjective going with both verbs — they come and go safe — where English reaches for an adverb.

sentences.t:
Telemus interea Siculam delatus ad Aetnen,
Telemus Eurymides, quem nulla fefellerat ales,
terribilem Polyphemon adit “lumen” que, “quod unum
fronte geris media, rapiet tibi” dixit “Ulixes!”
sentences.l: Telemus meanwhile, carried down to Sicilian Aetna, Telemus son of Eurymus, whom no bird had ever deceived, approaches the terrible Polyphemus and said, “The one light which you carry in the middle of your forehead — Ulysses will take it from you!”
sentences.i: Meanwhile Telemus, brought to Sicilian Etna — Telemus son of Eurymus, whom no bird ever misled — went up to the terrible Polyphemus and told him: “That one eye you carry in the middle of your forehead: Ulysses will take it from you.”
sentences.n: The ales that never deceived him is the bird of augury: Telemus is a seer, and the boast is that he never misread one. Aetnen and Polyphemon are Greek accusatives. The edition prints the enclitic detached and outside the quotation mark, “lumen” que, because it belongs to the quoted word but the quotation mark comes first; the same typography returns at 874 with “video” que. tibi is a dative of separation with rapiet, “will snatch from you”. adit is present and dixit perfect inside the one sentence, and the literal keeps both as they stand. Nothing in these lines says whether the prophecy comes true.

sentences.t:
Risit et “o vatum stolidissime, falleris,” inquit,
“altera iam rapuit!”
sentences.l: He laughed and said, “O most doltish of prophets, you are deceived; another woman has already carried it off!”
sentences.i: He laughed. “Stupidest of seers,” he said, “you are wrong — another has taken it already!”
sentences.n: falleris is passive, “you are deceived”, and it answers fefellerat three lines back at 771: the seer whom no bird ever deceived is told to his face that he is deceived. altera is feminine, “another woman”, and what she has taken is the lumen of 772 — the eye, and the light of it. stolidissime is a superlative in the vocative with the partitive genitive vatum.

sentences.t:
Sic frustra vera monentem
spernit et aut gradiens ingenti litora passu
degravat aut fessus sub opaca revertitur antra.
sentences.l: So he spurns the man warning true things in vain, and either, striding, weighs down the shores with his huge step, or, weary, returns beneath his shadowy caves.
sentences.i: So he brushed aside the man whose true warning was wasted, and went off — now tramping the shore, weighing it down with his enormous stride, now going back, tired, into his shadowy caves.
sentences.n: vera monentem is a participle used as a noun, “the man warning true things”, and it is the object of spernit; frustra belongs with monentem, so it is the warning that goes for nothing, not the spurning. degravat, “weighs down”, makes the beach feel the step. aut … aut sets out two habitual alternatives, and the present tenses here are narrative presents keeping the action in front of the reader.

sentences.t:
Prominet in pontum cuneatus acumine longo
collis utrumque latus circumfluit aequoris unda;
sentences.l: A hill juts out into the sea, wedge-shaped with a long point; the water of the sea flows round each side;
sentences.i: A hill runs out into the sea, tapering to a long wedge; the water flows round it on both sides;
sentences.n: cuneatus, “made into a wedge”, with acumine longo, the ablative of the point it narrows to. circumfluit is a compound that takes its object in the accusative directly, utrumque latus, “flows round both sides”. Magnus prints no stop at all between collis and utrumque, so the two clauses — the hill juts out, the water runs round it — stand side by side unpunctuated.

sentences.t:
huc ferus ascendit Cyclops mediusque resedit,
lanigerae pecudes nullo ducente secutae.
sentences.l: Up here the wild Cyclops climbed and settled in the middle, and his wool-bearing flocks followed, with none leading.
sentences.i: Up onto it the savage Cyclops climbed and sat down in the middle; his woolly sheep followed him, with nobody driving them.
sentences.n: medius is a predicative adjective, “as the middle one”, where English wants the adverbial “in the middle”. secutae is the perfect participle of the deponent sequor standing in for a finite verb: sunt is simply left out. nullo ducente is an ablative absolute built on a present participle, “with nobody leading” — the flock comes of its own accord.

sentences.t:
Cui postquam pinus, baculi quae praebuit usum,
ante pedes posita est, antemnis apta ferendis,
sumptaque harundinibus compacta est fistula centum,
sentences.l: For him, after the pine — which had furnished the use of a staff — was laid before his feet, fit for yardarms to be carried, and the pipe, joined together out of a hundred reeds, was taken up,
sentences.i: When the pine that served him for a walking-stick — a trunk big enough to carry a ship's yardarms — had been laid down at his feet, and he had taken up his pipe of a hundred reeds,
sentences.n: Cui is a dative of reference holding the whole postquam clause to Polyphemus, “for him”. postquam here takes the perfect indicative, posita est. The relative quae is postponed inside its own clause, after baculi. antemnis apta ferendis is a dative gerundive of purpose, “fit for yardarms to be carried” — the pine is mast-sized. sumpta and compacta share the single est, and harundinibus … centum is split apart around compacta est fistula.

sentences.t:
senserunt toti pastoria sibila montes,
senserunt undae;
sentences.l: The whole mountains felt the shepherd's whistlings, the waves felt them;
sentences.i: The mountains, all of them, felt the shepherd's piping; the waves felt it too;
sentences.n: senserunt is repeated at the head of two consecutive lines, 785 and 786. sentio of hills and water is “felt”, not “heard”: the sound is a physical thing that reaches them. toti montes is “the mountains entire”, and pastoria sibila a neuter plural, “shepherd-whistlings”.

sentences.t:
latitans ego rupe meique
Acidis in gremio residens procul auribus hausi
talia dicta meis auditaque verba notavi:
sentences.l: I, hiding on a rock and sitting in the lap of my own Acis, drank in from far off with my ears such words as these and noted the words I heard:
sentences.i: Hidden on a rock, sitting in my Acis's lap, I caught words like these from far off with my own ears, and took note of what I heard:
sentences.n: Two present participles, latitans and residens, hold the picture still while the two perfects hausi and notavi do the acting. rupe is a local ablative with no preposition. Two pairs are pulled apart across the line-end: mei is the last word of 786 and its noun Acidis the first of 787; auribus stands late in 787 and its adjective meis early in 788, with hausi talia dicta between them. haurio, “drain, drink up”, is used of taking sound in.

sentences.t:
“Candidior folio nivei, Galatea, ligustri,
floridior pratis, longa procerior alno,
splendidior vitro, tenero lascivior haedo,
sentences.l: “Whiter, Galatea, than the leaf of the snowy privet, more flowering than the meadows, taller than the long alder, more shining than glass, friskier than a tender kid,
sentences.i: “Galatea, whiter than a snow-white privet leaf, more in bloom than meadows, taller than the tall alder, brighter than glass, more playful than a young kid,
sentences.n: The song opens on a chain of comparatives in the vocative, all agreeing with Galatea, and each takes a plain ablative of comparison — folio, pratis, alno, vitro, haedo — where English needs “than”. The vocative Galatea is wedged inside the very phrase that praises her, between nivei and its noun ligustri. In longa procerior alno the adjective longa agrees with alno, so the comparison concedes the alder's height before overtopping it.

sentences.t:
levior adsiduo detritis aequore conchis,
solibus hibernis, aestiva gratior umbra,
nobilior pomis, platano conspectior alta,
lucidior glacie, matura dulcior uva,
sentences.l: smoother than shells rubbed away by the ceaseless sea, more welcome than winter suns, than summer shade, more prized than fruit, more striking than a tall plane, brighter than ice, sweeter than a ripe grape,
sentences.i: smoother than shells the sea has worn ceaselessly, more welcome than winter sun, than summer shade, finer than orchard fruit, more striking than a tall plane tree, clearer than ice, sweeter than a ripe grape,
sentences.n: detritis … conchis is the ablative of comparison with its participle inside it, and adsiduo aequore the ablative of what does the wearing. gratior in 793 governs two ablatives at once, solibus hibernis and aestiva umbra: welcome as sun is in winter and shade in summer. Magnus prints nobilior pomis, “more prized than fruit”; some editions print mobilior damma, “nimbler than a doe”, which changes the item from a compliment on worth to one on movement.

sentences.t:
mollior et cygni plumis et lacte coacto
et, si non fugias, riguo formosior horto
sentences.l: softer both than the swan's feathers and than curdled milk, and, if you would not flee, more beautiful than a watered garden,
sentences.i: softer than swan's down and than fresh curds, and — if only you would not run — lovelier than a watered garden,
sentences.n: et … et pairs the two ablatives of comparison, “both … and”. lac coactum is milk driven together, that is, curds. si non fugias is a present subjunctive in a should-would condition, and it is the first crack in the praise: the wish that she would not run is slipped inside a compliment. Magnus prints no punctuation whatever at the end of 797, so the turn from praise to abuse in the next line comes with no stop before it.

sentences.t:
saevior indomitis eadem Galatea iuvencis,
durior annosa quercu, fallacior undis,
lentior et salicis virgis et vitibus albis,
sentences.l: fiercer than untamed bullocks, the same Galatea, harder than an aged oak, more treacherous than the waves, more pliant both than willow's withies and than white vine-shoots,
sentences.i: and fiercer than unbroken bullocks, the same Galatea — harder than an old oak, falser than the sea, suppler than willow withies or white bryony,
sentences.n: eadem, “the same woman”, is the hinge of the song: the person just praised is the person now abused, and the grammar does not change with the tone — the comparatives run straight on. lentus covers both “pliant, tough”, which is what a withy is, and “unmoved, cool”, the regular Latin word for a lover who will not respond; the comparison lives on both senses at once. vitis alba, the white vine, is usually taken to be bryony. fallacior undis makes waves the type of what cannot be trusted, and waves are her own element.

sentences.t:
his inmobilior scopulis, violentior amne,
laudato pavone superbior, acrior igni,
asperior tribulis, feta truculentior ursa,
surdior aequoribus, calcato inmitior hydro,
sentences.l: more immovable than these crags, more violent than a river, prouder than a peacock when praised, keener than fire, rougher than caltrops, more savage than a she-bear with young, deafer than the open seas, more merciless than a water-snake trodden on,
sentences.i: more unbudging than these rocks, more violent than a river in flood, prouder than a peacock being admired, sharper than fire, rougher than a caltrop, fiercer than a she-bear with cubs, deafer than the sea, crueller than a trodden water-snake,
sentences.n: his scopulis, “these crags”, is deictic: he is sitting on the headland described at 778–780 and points at it. laudato pavone and calcato hydro each pack a whole clause into an ablative of comparison — “than a peacock when it is praised”, “than a water-snake when it is trodden on”. feta ursa is a she-bear that has given birth, the stock example of a dangerous animal. surdior aequoribus insults her with the element she lives in: the sea does not hear, and neither does she.

sentences.t: et, quod praecipue vellem tibi demere possem.
sentences.l: and — what above all I should wish I were able to take from you —
sentences.i: and — the one thing I would most wish I could take away from you —
sentences.n: vellem and possem are both imperfect subjunctives of the polite unreal, “I could wish I were able”; the second depends on the first without any connecting word. The relative quod looks forward, not back: what he would take from her is the fleeing named in the next lines. As Magnus prints it, 805 closes with a full stop, which leaves 806–807 standing as a sentence with no verb of their own, still agreeing with the vocative Galatea of 789. Shipped as printed.

sentences.t:
Non tantum cervo claris latratibus acto,
verum etiam ventis volucrique fugacior aura!
sentences.l: more fleeting not only than a stag driven by clear bayings, but even than the winds and than the winged breeze!
sentences.i: more fleeting not only than a stag driven on by the clear baying of hounds, but than the winds, than the breeze on the wing!
sentences.n: fugacior is the last word but one of 807 and reaches back to govern everything from cervo onwards: more fleeting than the stag, than the winds, than the breeze. English cannot hold a comparative that long, so the literal brings it to the front, where it can cover both limbs at once. non tantum … verum etiam is prose idiom fitted into the hexameter; the same frame comes again at 817–818 with solum for tantum. claris latratibus is the ablative of means of the driving, clarus of sound being “clear, ringing”. volucris aura makes the moving air itself a winged thing.

sentences.t:
At bene si noris, pigeat fugisse morasque
ipsa tuas damnes et me retinere labores.
sentences.l: But if you knew me well, it would irk you to have fled, and you yourself would condemn your own delays and would take pains to hold me.
sentences.i: But if you knew me properly, you would be sorry you ever ran; you would blame your own dawdling and work hard to keep me.
sentences.n: noris is syncopated for noveris, and the perfect of nosco has present meaning, “know”. The apodosis carries three present subjunctives, pigeat, damnes, labores — the should-would condition of an imagined case. pigeat is impersonal with the infinitive fugisse, “it would irk you to have fled”. laboro with the infinitive retinere is “take trouble to”. ipsa, feminine, throws the fault back on her.

sentences.l: There are to me — a part of the mountain — caves hanging in the living rock, in which neither is the sun felt in the middle of the heat nor is winter felt;
sentences.i: I have caves, a piece of the mountain itself, hanging in the living rock, where you feel neither the sun at the height of summer nor the winter;
sentences.n: Sunt mihi is the dative of possession, “there are to me” = “I have”, and it starts an inventory: sunt comes four times over in 810–814 and twice more at 827–828. pars montis is a nominative in apposition dropped into the middle of the clause. vivum saxum is rock still in place, unquarried. quibus is a plain local ablative, “in which”, and sentitur is repeated for each half of the nec … nec.

sentences.t:
sunt poma gravantia ramos,
sunt auro similes longis in vitibus uvae,
sunt et purpureae: tibi et has servamus et illas.
sentences.l: there are fruits weighing down the branches, there are grapes like gold on the long vines, and there are purple ones too: both these and those we keep for you.
sentences.i: there is fruit weighing the branches down, there are grapes like gold on the long vines, and purple ones as well — I am keeping both sorts for you.
sentences.n: poma is fruit of any tree, not apples in particular. similis takes the dative, auro. tibi et has … et illas is the “both … and” pairing again, here across the two colours of grape. servamus is a plural used by a single speaker of himself, as succumbimus is at 856 and nostra at 839; the literal keeps the plural everywhere the Latin has it, and the idiomatic turns it back into the one man who is speaking.

sentences.t:
Ipsa tuis manibus silvestri nata sub umbra
mollia fraga leges, ipsa autumnalia corna
prunaque, non solum nigro liventia suco,
verum etiam generosa novasque imitantia ceras.
sentences.l: You yourself with your own hands will pick soft strawberries born beneath the woodland shade, you yourself the autumn cornel-berries and plums, not only those livid with dark juice but also the choice kind that imitate fresh wax.
sentences.i: With your own hands you will gather soft strawberries grown in the woodland shade; you yourself will pick autumn cornel-berries and plums — not only the ones dark with purple juice, but the fine sort too, the colour of new wax.
sentences.n: Ipsa … ipsa, repeated, is the whole point of the offer: she is to do the picking herself. leges is the future of lego, “gather”, and the one verb serves both halves of the sentence. nata, “born”, is used of fruit coming on. liventia takes suco as an ablative of cause, the blue-black of the dark plum; new wax is pale yellow, so the second kind is the yellow plum, and imitantia takes ceras as a direct object. non solum … verum etiam is the same frame as at 806–807, with solum in place of tantum.

sentences.t:
Nec tibi castaneae me coniuge, nec tibi deerunt
arbutei fetus: omnis tibi serviet arbor.
sentences.l: Nor, with me as your husband, will chestnuts fail you, nor the arbutus's fruits: every tree will be a slave to you.
sentences.i: With me for a husband you will never go short of chestnuts, nor of arbutus berries: every tree will be at your service.
sentences.n: me coniuge is an ablative absolute built out of two nouns and no participle at all, “with me as husband”, where English wants a clause. deerunt is the future of desum with the dative tibi, “be lacking to you”, and the double nec … nec spreads it over both subjects; the verb closes 819 while its second subject, arbutei fetus, does not arrive until 820. serviet, “will be a slave”, keeps the whole offer in the language of ownership.

sentences.t:
Hoc pecus omne meum est, multae quoque vallibus errant,
multas silva tegit, multae stabulantur in antris.
sentences.l: All this flock is mine, and many also wander in the valleys, many the wood covers, many are stalled in caves.
sentences.i: All this flock is mine — and there are many more roaming the valleys, many the wood hides, many housed in caves.
sentences.n: multae, multas, multae are feminine although pecus is neuter: the gender slips from the flock as a body to the ewes in it. quoque here is the plain adverb, “also”; the same letters can be quo-que, “and with which”, so the word is worth a second look each time it appears — it is the adverb again at 828 and at 896. vallibus is a local ablative with no preposition, standing beside in antris with one, in the same sentence.

sentences.t: Nec, si forte roges, possim tibi dicere, quot sint:
sentences.l: Nor, if you should happen to ask, could I tell you how many there are:
sentences.i: And if you happened to ask, I could not tell you how many there are:
sentences.n: possim is the potential subjunctive, “I could”; roges is the subjunctive of the protasis, “should you ask”, with si forte, “if by chance”. quot sint is an indirect question with the subjunctive. The modesty is a boast: not being able to count them is the point.

sentences.t: pauperis est numerare pecus!
sentences.l: it belongs to a poor man to count his flock!
sentences.i: counting the flock is a poor man's business!
sentences.n: The genitive of characteristic: pauperis est with an infinitive is “it is the mark of a poor man to …”, a construction that puts the whole judgement into one case-ending. The line stands on its own as a sententia, and the boast is that he is too rich to bother.

sentences.t:
De laudibus harum
nil mihi credideris:
sentences.l: About the praises of these you should believe me in nothing:
sentences.i: Do not take my word for anything I say in their praise:
sentences.n: credideris is a perfect subjunctive used as a mild prohibition, “do not believe” — the perfect, not the present, is the idiom for a negative command of this kind, and nil supplies the negative. mihi is the dative that credo takes of the person believed and nil an internal accusative, so the Latin is “believe me in nothing”, not “receive nothing from me”. harum is feminine, picking up the ewes of 821–822 rather than the neuter pecus.

sentences.t:
praesens potes ipse videre,
ut vix circueant distentum cruribus uber.
sentences.l: you can see for yourself, being on the spot, how they scarcely get their legs round the swollen udder.
sentences.i: come and see for yourself: they can hardly get their legs round the swollen udder.
sentences.n: praesens is a predicative adjective, “present, on the spot”, doing the work of a whole clause. ut with the subjunctive circueant after videre is “see how …”, an indirect exclamation. distentum uber is the stretched udder, and cruribus the ablative of the legs that barely reach round it. Magnus prints ipse, masculine, though the whole song is addressed to Galatea; some editions print ipsa, agreeing with her. Shipped as printed, and rendered “for yourself”, which takes no gender either way.

sentences.t:
Sunt, fetura minor, tepidis in ovilibus agni,
sunt quoque, par aetas, aliis in ovilibus haedi.
sentences.l: There are lambs, the smaller breeding, in warm sheepfolds; there are also kids, an equal age, in other folds.
sentences.i: There are lambs — the younger crop — in the warm folds, and kids too, of the same age, in other folds.
sentences.n: fetura minor and par aetas are nominatives in apposition thrown into the middle of their own clauses, each compressing a whole remark about the animals into two words. The existential sunt carries on the inventory begun at 810. In both halves the preposition sits between adjective and noun, tepidis in ovilibus, aliis in ovilibus.

sentences.t:
Lac mihi semper adest niveum: pars inde bibenda
servatur, partem liquefacta coagula durant.
sentences.l: Snowy milk is always at hand for me: part of it is kept to be drunk, part the melted rennet hardens.
sentences.i: I always have snow-white milk: some is kept for drinking, and some the dissolved rennet sets into cheese.
sentences.n: adest takes the dative mihi, “is at hand for me”. bibenda is a gerundive marking what the kept part is for, “to be drunk”. pars is nominative and partem accusative because the construction changes under them: the first is subject of the passive servatur, the second object of the active durant, which here is transitive, “make hard”. liquefacta coagula, “melted curdling-stuff”, is rennet.

sentences.t:
Nec tibi deliciae faciles vulgataque tantum
munera contingent, dammae leporesque caperque
parve columbarum demptusve cacumine nidus:
sentences.l: Nor will easy dainties and merely common gifts fall to you — does and hares and a he-goat, or a pair of doves, or a nest taken down from a treetop:
sentences.i: And you will not be getting cheap treats and nothing but the usual presents — does, hares, a billy-goat, a pair of doves, a nest lifted out of a treetop:
sentences.n: contingent is the future of contingo with the dative tibi, “fall to your lot”. tantum, “only”, belongs with vulgata munera, and Nec negates the lot: what he offers is not the ordinary stuff. parve is not a vocative but par with the enclitic -ve, “or a pair”, answered by demptus-ve; the two -ve's offer alternatives inside a list otherwise strung on -que. cacumine is an ablative of separation with demptus.

sentences.t:
inveni geminos, qui tecum ludere possint,
inter se similes, vix ut dignoscere possis,
villosae catulos in summis montibus ursae,
inveni et dixi “dominae servabimus istos!”
sentences.l: I have found twins, such as could play with you, alike to each other, so that you could scarcely tell them apart, cubs of a shaggy she-bear on the mountain-tops — I found them and said, “These we shall keep for our mistress!”
sentences.i: I have found you twins to play with, so alike that you could hardly tell them apart — bear cubs, a shaggy mother's, high in the mountains. I found them and said, “These I shall keep for my mistress!”
sentences.n: inveni opens 834 and comes again at the start of 837, with the whole object, geminos … catulos … ursae, spread out between the two: the sentence circles back to its own verb. qui … possint and vix ut … possis are both subjunctives of characteristic and result, “such as could play”, “so alike that you could hardly”; ut is postponed after vix inside its own clause. istos is the demonstrative of the second person, “those of yours”, pointing them at her before she has them. domina is the mistress of a household and also the standard word for the woman a lover treats as his owner.

sentences.t:
Iam modo caeruleo nitidum caput exsere ponto,
iam, Galatea, veni, nec munera despice nostra.
sentences.l: Now only lift your shining head out of the dark-blue sea, now, Galatea, come, and do not despise our gifts.
sentences.i: Only lift that bright head of yours out of the blue sea now; come now, Galatea, and do not turn up your nose at my gifts.
sentences.n: modo with the imperative is “only, just”, making the request as small as he can. caeruleo ponto is an ablative of separation with exsere, ex-sero, “put out from”. iam opens each of the two lines, 838 and 839. nec with the imperative despice is the poets' negative command, where prose would use noli or ne. nostra is the plural of a single speaker again, as at 814.

sentences.t:
Certe ego me novi liquidaeque in imagine vidi
nuper aquae, placuitque mihi mea forma videnti.
sentences.l: Certainly I know myself, and lately I saw myself in the image of clear water, and my own shape pleased me as I looked.
sentences.i: I certainly know myself: not long ago I saw myself in the reflection of clear water, and I liked the look of my own shape.
sentences.n: novi is the perfect of nosco and means “I know”. liquidae and its noun aquae are split across the line-end: liquidae stands in the middle of 840 and aquae in 841, with in imagine vidi nuper standing between them. videnti is a dative participle agreeing with the mihi of placuit, “pleased me as I looked”.

sentences.t:
Adspice, sim quantus! Non est hoc corpore maior
Iuppiter in caelo:
sentences.l: Look, how big I am! Jupiter in heaven is not bigger than this body:
sentences.i: Look how big I am! Jupiter in the sky is no bigger than this body:
sentences.n: sim quantus is an indirect question after adspice, with the subjunctive and the order turned round, “look how great I may be”. hoc corpore is an ablative of comparison with maior. Adspice keeps the edition's own spelling with adsp-, which is not normalised here.

sentences.t:
nam vos narrare soletis,
nescio quem regnare Iovem.
sentences.l: for you people are accustomed to tell that some Jupiter or other reigns.
sentences.i: for you lot are always saying that some Jupiter or other is king.
sentences.n: vos is contemptuous — “you people”, the sea-folk and their stories — and both layers keep the contempt, which is the Cyclops's and not the poem's. nescio quem is the frozen indefinite, “some … or other”; nescio has stopped being a verb here and is not construed with a question. narrare takes the accusative and infinitive, with nescio quem … Iovem as its one accusative subject of regnare, and soletis with the infinitive is “you are in the habit of”.

sentences.t:
Coma plurima torvos
prominet in vultus umerosque, ut lucus, obumbrat.
sentences.l: Very abundant hair juts out over my grim face and shades my shoulders, like a grove.
sentences.i: My hair, thick as it grows, hangs out over my grim face and shades my shoulders like a wood.
sentences.n: plurima is the superlative of multus used of quantity, “in the greatest abundance”. torvos vultus is an accusative plural for the single face. prominet in with the accusative is “juts out over” — the same verb used at 778 of the headland he is sitting on, now used of himself. ut lucus is a compressed comparison with the verb left out, “as a grove does”.

sentences.l: And do not think it ugly that my body, thickest-set, bristles with stiff hairs — ugly is a tree without leaves, ugly a horse, unless manes veil its yellow neck;
sentences.i: And do not think it ugly that my body bristles thick with stiff hair. A tree is ugly without leaves; a horse is ugly unless a mane covers its golden neck;
sentences.n: Nec … puta is the poetic negative command again, as nec despice was at 839. turpe is a predicative accusative with puta, and the quod-clause is the thing being called ugly. mea corpora is a poetic plural for one body, and it is torn across the line-end: mea and densissima both stand in 846 while their noun corpora is the first word of 847. horrent, “stand on end, bristle”, takes the ablative saetis. est is left out of both following clauses, and in 848 colla and flaventia are split around iubae.

sentences.t:
pluma tegit volucres, ovibus sua lana decori est
barba viros hirtaeque decent in corpore saetae.
sentences.l: feathers cover birds, their own wool is for a glory to sheep; a beard and shaggy bristles on the body become men.
sentences.i: Feathers clothe birds, a sheep's own wool is its glory, and a beard and rough bristles on the body are what suit a man.
sentences.n: ovibus sua lana decori est is the double dative: decori is the dative of purpose, “for a glory”, and ovibus the dative of the ones concerned. decent takes the accusative of the person suited, viros, with barba and saetae as its plural subjects — English has to turn the sentence round. Magnus prints no stop between decori est and barba, so those clauses run together with nothing between them.

sentences.t:
Unum est in media lumen mihi fronte, sed instar
ingentis clipei.
sentences.l: There is one light for me in the middle of my forehead, but the size of a huge shield.
sentences.i: I have one eye in the middle of my forehead — but it is the size of a great shield.
sentences.n: lumen, “light”, is the word for the eye, and it is the word Telemus used of it at 772; the phrase for its place is all but the same, fronte … media standing together in 773 there and in media … fronte split around lumen mihi here. mihi is a dative of possession. instar is an indeclinable neuter noun, “the equivalent, the bulk”, governing the genitive ingentis clipei and standing in apposition to lumen with no verb of its own.

sentences.t:
Quid? non haec omnia magnus
Sol videt e caelo? Soli tamen unicus orbis!
sentences.l: What of it? Does not the great Sun see all these things from heaven? Yet to the Sun there is one disc only!
sentences.i: So what? Does not the great Sun see all this from the sky? And the Sun has just one disc!
sentences.n: Quid? is the rhetorical “what of it?” that brushes an objection aside before it is made. non … videt is a question expecting the answer yes. Soli is a dative of possession with est left out, which is why the literal keeps “to the Sun there is”; orbis is the round face of the Sun and, by the argument he is making, an eye. The reasoning is his own: one eye, like the Sun's one round face.

sentences.t: Adde, quod in vestro genitor meus aequore regnat:
sentences.l: Add this, that my father reigns in your sea:
sentences.i: Add this too: my father is king in your own sea —
sentences.n: Adde quod is the prose formula for piling on one more argument, and it takes the indicative, regnat. vestro is the plural “your”, of her whole kind, where the rest of the speech uses the singular tuus of Galatea alone: he is claiming kinship with the sea-people at large. The father is not named in these lines; what is said of him is only that he reigns in her water.

sentences.t:
hunc tibi do socerum; tantum miserere precesque
supplicis exaudi! tibi enim succumbimus uni.
sentences.l: him I give to you as a father-in-law; only take pity, and hear out the prayers of a suppliant! For to you alone do we submit.
sentences.i: Him I give you for a father-in-law; only take pity, and hear a suppliant's prayer to the end! For you are the only one I bow to.
sentences.n: do … socerum is a double accusative, “I give him as a father-in-law”, with tibi the person given to. miserere is the imperative of the deponent misereor. exaudi, with its ex-, is “hear out, hear to the end”, stronger than audi. supplicis is the genitive of supplex, one who kneels. succumbimus is the plural of a single speaker again, and uni is the dative of unus agreeing with tibi, “to you alone”.

sentences.t:
Quique Iovem et caelum sperno et penetrabile fulmen,
Nerei, te veneror: tua fulmine saevior ira est. —
sentences.l: And I, who despise Jupiter and heaven and the piercing thunderbolt, I worship you, daughter of Nereus: your anger is fiercer than the thunderbolt. —
sentences.i: And I, who scorn Jupiter and heaven and the thunderbolt that pierces anything — you, daughter of Nereus, I worship: your anger is fiercer than any thunderbolt. —
sentences.n: Quique is the relative with -que attached, opening the sentence as a connecting relative, “and I, who …”; the antecedent is only the unexpressed ego inside veneror, which is why sperno is first person. Nerei is the vocative of Nereis, “daughter of Nereus”. penetrabile is active in force, “able to pierce”, not “able to be pierced”. Magnus prints veneror, “I worship”; some editions print vereor, “I fear”, which makes the line a confession instead of an act of worship. Magnus marks the turn of thought with an em dash.

sentences.t:
Atque ego contemptus essem patientior huius,
si fugeres omnes;
sentences.l: And I would be more tolerant of this contempt, if you fled from everyone;
sentences.i: And I could bear this contempt better if you ran from everybody;
sentences.n: essem and fugeres are imperfect subjunctives of an unreal condition about the present, “I would be … if you were fleeing”. patientior takes an objective genitive, contemptus … huius, and the noun and its demonstrative are split around the verb: contemptus stands before essem, huius closes the line.

sentences.t:
sed cur Cyclope repulso
Acin amas praefersque meis complexibus Acin?
sentences.l: but why, with the Cyclops rejected, do you love Acis, and prefer Acis to my embraces?
sentences.i: But why, having turned the Cyclops down, do you love Acis — prefer Acis to my arms?
sentences.n: Cyclope repulso is an ablative absolute, and he puts his own name into it as though speaking of somebody else. praefero takes the accusative of what is preferred, Acin, and the dative of what it is preferred to, meis complexibus. Acin is the Greek accusative of Acis, and the name stands at both ends of 861 — first word and last word of the line.

sentences.t:
Ille tamen placeatque sibi placeatque licebit,
quod nollem, Galatea, tibi;
sentences.l: Yet he may please himself and please you — which I should not wish, Galatea;
sentences.i: Still, let him please himself and please you too — and I would rather he did not, Galatea;
sentences.n: licebit with the bare subjunctive placeat, no ut between them, is a concession: “he may, for all that”. The paired -que … -que hangs two datives on the repeated verb, sibi and tibi. quod nollem is a parenthesis with the imperfect subjunctive of polite unwillingness, “which I could wish otherwise”; it pushes tibi out of 862 altogether, so the second dative arrives only in the next line after the vocative.

sentences.t:
modo copia detur,
sentiet esse mihi tanto pro corpore vires!
sentences.l: only let the chance be given, and he will feel that there is strength in me to match so great a body!
sentences.i: just give me the chance, and he will find out that my strength matches a body this size!
sentences.n: modo with the subjunctive detur is a wish doing the work of a condition, “if only the chance be given”. sentiet takes the accusative and infinitive esse … vires, with mihi a dative of possession, so the literal keeps the existential shape rather than making him the subject of a verb “have”. pro with the ablative here is “in proportion to, to match”, not “on behalf of”.

sentences.t:
Viscera viva traham divisaque membra per agros
perque tuas spargam (sic se tibi misceat!) undas.
sentences.l: I will drag his entrails out living and scatter his divided limbs through the fields and through your waters — so let him mingle with you! —
sentences.i: I will drag his guts out alive and scatter his dismembered limbs over the fields and through your water — let him mix with you like that! —
sentences.n: viva is predicative and the horror sits in it: the entrails are alive as he drags them. divisa is the perfect participle of divido, “divided”, the limbs parted from the body; some editions print divulsa, “torn away”, which is the more violent word. The preposition is repeated with -que, per … perque, spreading the scattering over land and water alike. sic se tibi misceat is a parenthetical jussive subjunctive, which Magnus prints inside round brackets; it turns her own element into the instrument of the killing. tuas comes near the head of 866 and undas is the last word of the line, with the whole parenthesis standing between them.

sentences.t:
Uror enim, laesusque exaestuat acrior ignis,
cumque suis videor translatam viribus Aetnam
pectore ferre meo: nec tu, Galatea, moveris.”
sentences.l: For I am burned, and the fire, struck at, boils up fiercer, and I seem to carry Aetna, moved across with all her force, in my breast: and you, Galatea, are not moved.”
sentences.i: For I am burning, and the fire, hurt, boils up hotter still, and I feel as if I were carrying Etna, force and all, shifted into my chest — and you, Galatea, are not moved.”
sentences.n: Uror is passive, “I am burned”, and it picks up uritur at 763, where the same fire was described from the outside; here he says it of himself. laesus agrees with ignis: a fire that is struck at only blazes higher. videor with the infinitive ferre is personal, “I seem to carry”, where English often prefers “it seems that I …”. translatam Aetnam with cum suis viribus is the mountain carried bodily across into his chest. moveris is present passive, “you are not stirred”. The English uses the one word moved for the mountain and for her; the Latin uses two, transfero of Aetna carried across and moveo of the woman who does not stir, and the pairing is the point.

sentences.t:
Talia nequiquam questus (nam cuncta videbam)
surgit et ut taurus vacca furibundus adempta,
stare nequit silvaque et notis saltibus errat:
sentences.l: Having complained of such things in vain — for I saw it all — he rises and, like a bull raging when his cow has been taken away, cannot stand still, and wanders over the wood and the glades he knows:
sentences.i: Having made all that complaint for nothing — I saw the whole of it — he got up, and like a bull gone mad because his cow has been taken from him he could not stand still, but roamed the wood and the passes he knew:
sentences.n: questus is the perfect participle of the deponent queror, active in force, with talia as its internal object, “having complained such things”. nam cuncta videbam is Galatea stepping back into her own narration inside a parenthesis, reminding the listener whose account this is. vacca adempta is an ablative absolute inside the simile, and furibundus stands between its two words. silva and saltibus are local ablatives with no preposition after errat.

sentences.t:
cum ferus ignaros nec quicquam tale timentes
me videt atque Acin “video” que exclamat “et ista
ultima sit, faciam, veneris concordia vestrae!”
sentences.l: when the savage one sees me and Acis, unaware and fearing nothing of the kind, and shouts, “I see you — and that concord of your love-making, I will bring it about, shall be the last!”
sentences.i: when the brute caught sight of us — me and Acis, off our guard, fearing nothing of the sort — and roared, “I see you! And I will see to it that this is the last coupling the two of you ever have!”
sentences.n: cum here is the inverted cum of narrative, “when suddenly”, and the sentence turns on it: videt is present, like surgit, nequit and errat before it in 871–872, so the whole turn is carried in the historic present. ignaros and timentes are accusative plurals covering me atque Acin together, so the plural takes in the pair although me is singular. faciam governs the bare subjunctive sit with no ut, “I will bring it about that it be”, and it sits inside its own clause as a parenthesis. ista is the demonstrative of the second person, “that of yours”, contemptuous here; venus is the act and not the goddess, and concordia veneris is the coming together of it. The edition again prints the enclitic outside the quotation mark, “video” que, as it did at 772.

sentences.t:
Tantaque vox, quantam Cyclops iratus habere
debuit, illa fuit: clamore perhorruit Aetne.
sentences.l: And that voice of his was as great as an angry Cyclops was bound to have: Aetna shuddered right through at the shout.
sentences.i: And it was as big a voice as an angry Cyclops was bound to have: Etna shuddered from end to end at the shout.
sentences.n: Tanta … quantam is the correlative pair, “as great … as”; illa, “that voice”, is held back and only closes the clause. debuit is of what is owed by fitness rather than by obligation, “was bound to have”. The per- in perhorruit carries the shudder right through the mountain. Aetne is the Greek nominative; the edition prints the Greek accusative Aetnen at 770 but the Latin Aetnam at 868, so both declensions of the name stand in this part.

sentences.t:
Ast ego vicino pavefacta sub aequore mergor,
terga fugae dederat conversa Symaethius heros
et “fer opem, Galatea, precor, mihi! ferte, parentes”
dixerat “et vestris periturum admittite regnis!”
sentences.l: But I, terrified, plunge beneath the water near by; the Symaethian hero had given his turned back to flight, and had said, “Bring help to me, Galatea, I beg! Bring help, parents, and take into your kingdoms one who is about to die!”
sentences.i: But I, in terror, dived under the sea that was close at hand. The hero of Symaethus had turned tail and run, and had cried, “Help me, Galatea, I beg you! Help me, parents — take a man about to die into your realms!”
sentences.n: Ast is the older, poetic form of at, “but”. pavefacta is feminine, agreeing with Galatea's ego. mergor is passive in form but used with middle force, “I plunge myself under”. terga dare fugae is the idiom for turning tail; conversa is neuter plural agreeing with terga, which is itself a poetic plural for the one back. The two pluperfects dederat and dixerat put both of his actions before the moment of her diving in 878: she tells her own escape first, then goes back to what he had already done. Symaethius names Acis by the river of the nymph called Symaethis at 750. periturum is the future participle used as a noun, “one who is going to die”, the object of admittite, with vestris regnis dative after the compound.

sentences.t:
Insequitur Cyclops partemque e monte revulsam
mittit, et extremus quamvis pervenit ad illum,
angulus is molis totum tamen obruit Acin.
sentences.l: The Cyclops pursues and throws a piece torn away out of the mountain, and although it reached him as its outermost part, that corner of the mass nevertheless buried the whole of Acis.
sentences.i: The Cyclops came after him and threw a piece torn out of the mountain; and although only its far edge reached him, that corner of the mass was enough to bury the whole of Acis.
sentences.n: revulsam is the perfect participle of revello, “torn away”, with e monte. quamvis takes the indicative pervenit here rather than the subjunctive. extremus and its noun angulus are split across the line-end: extremus stands early in 883 and angulus is the first word of 884, with quamvis pervenit ad illum between them, so the reader learns only afterwards what the thing that reached him was. totum agrees with Acin, not with the mass: it is Acis who is covered entire.

sentences.t:
At nos, quod fieri solum per fata licebat,
fecimus, ut vires adsumeret Acis avitas.
sentences.l: But we did the only thing that through the fates was allowed to be done: that Acis should take on his grandfather's powers.
sentences.i: But we did the one thing the fates allowed to be done: Acis took on his grandfather's powers.
sentences.n: nos and fecimus are Galatea's plural for herself, the same usage the Cyclops used of himself at 856. The relative clause quod … licebat is the object of fecimus and stands before its verb, “we did the thing which …”; quod itself is the subject of the infinitive fieri. per fata is “by way of, through the fates”, that is, as far as fate allowed. The ut-clause then says what the thing was. avitas, “a grandfather's”, points back through his mother, the nymph of the Symaethus at 750, so what he takes on is water; vires and avitas are split apart around adsumeret Acis.

sentences.t:
Puniceus de mole cruor manabat, et intra
temporis exiguum rubor evanescere coepit
fitque color primo turbati fluminis imbre
purgaturque mora;
sentences.l: Crimson gore was flowing from the mass, and within a little of time the redness began to vanish, and the colour becomes that of a river troubled by the first rain, and it is cleared by the delay;
sentences.i: Crimson blood was running out from under the mass, and in a little while the red began to fade; the colour turned to that of a river muddied by the first rain, and it cleared as time passed;
sentences.n: intra temporis exiguum is a neuter adjective used as a noun with a partitive genitive, “within a little of time”. The tenses change under the change they describe: imperfect manabat, then the perfect coepit, then the presents fit and purgatur taking over as it happens. In primo turbati fluminis imbre, turbati agrees with fluminis and imbre is the ablative of what does the troubling; the whole is a compressed comparison, the colour of a river after the first rain. mora is an ablative of means, “by the delay”.

sentences.t:
tum moles tacta dehiscit,
vivaque per rimas proceraque surgit harundo,
osque cavum saxi sonat exsultantibus undis:
sentences.l: then the mass, touched, gapes apart, and a reed, living and tall, rises through the cracks, and the hollow mouth of the rock sounds with leaping waters:
sentences.i: then the mass, at a touch, splits open; a reed, alive and tall, comes up through the cracks; and the hollow mouth of the rock sounds with water leaping out:
sentences.n: tacta is a perfect participle with no agent named: what touched the mass is not said. Magnus prints tacta, “touched”; some editions print iacta, “thrown”, which would make it simply the mass he had hurled and take the touch away altogether. viva and procera are both joined to harundo by -que, one on each side of per rimas. os is the mouth of a face and also the mouth of a spring; cavum agrees with os and not with saxi, so what sounds is the rock's own hollow mouth. exsultantibus undis is an ablative of means with sonat. exs- is the edition's spelling and is kept as printed.

sentences.t:
miraque res, subito media tenus exstitit alvo
incinctus iuvenis flexis nova cornua cannis,
qui, nisi quod maior, quod toto caerulus ore,
Acis erat.
sentences.l: and — a marvellous thing — suddenly, as far as the middle of his belly, there stood forth a young man girt as to his new horns with bent reeds, who, except that he was bigger, except that he was dark-blue over his whole face, was Acis.
sentences.i: And — a marvel — suddenly, up to the middle of his waist, a young man stood out of the water, his new horns wreathed with bent reeds; and he, except that he was bigger, and blue over the whole of his face, was Acis.
sentences.n: mira res is a nominative exclamation dropped into the sentence without any verb of its own. tenus is a postposition: it follows media, and its noun alvo is held back past the verb to the end of the line. nova cornua is a Greek accusative of respect after the passive participle incinctus — “girt as to his new horns” — the accusative naming the part affected, the first of its kind in this part; flexis cannis is the ablative of what does the girding, and flexis … cannis is split around nova cornua. nisi quod … quod gives two exceptions in turn, each a clause of its own. exstitit keeps the edition's exs- spelling.

sentences.t:
Sed sic quoque erat tamen Acis, in amnem
versus, et antiquum tenuerunt flumina nomen.”
sentences.l: But even so he was Acis still, turned into a river, and the waters kept their old name.”
sentences.i: But even so he was still Acis, turned into a river — and the stream kept its old name.”
sentences.n: sic quoque is “even so, in this way too”, with quoque the adverb again, not quo-que. versus is the perfect participle of verto, passive, and it agrees with Acis, from whom the line-end separates it: Acis and then in amnem close 896, and versus opens 897. flumina is a neuter plural for the single stream. The closing quotation mark here shuts the speech the edition opened at 750, so Galatea has been the speaker of every word of these lines.
